name: December
blurb: Closing lines, and the promise the books keep: the last sentence opens on a beginning.
rules: A line from a NAMED WORK by a named author, philosophy or imaginative literature, first published before 2000.
Famous, meaning one of: the opening or closing line of a work; the sentence the work is known by; a locatable entry in a standard reference (a fame signal, never a verification).
It must help at six in the morning on this month's theme. Famous and bleak is out.

Every candidate carries a LOCATABLE citation before it is proposed: work, and book/chapter/letter/section/line, or edition and page. A translated line names the translator and year of the published translation whose wording it uses.

The source line LEADS with the author's name (the card prints it as the byline and has no author field), then the work, then the locator, then the translation in parentheses. A character's line names the speaker in parentheses after the locator. At most 140 characters. No em dash in the source or the note: use a colon.
The quotation ends in a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. Curly quotes only; no straight double quote anywhere.

VERSE keeps its line breaks, marked " / " (a slash with a space each side), in the lineation of the edition named, with the poem's own capitals at the line head. A verse quotation is never run together as prose. Prose is never broken into lines.
No person twice in the month; at most three lines per person in the year. Authors on the banned list never.

Per month the editor balances: at most 10 entries from one country, at most 16 originally written in English, at least 8 women, at least 4 of the 7 tags, at least 3 centuries. Curators recruit toward that: name translators, go beyond the English canon.
Nothing already shipped in Q, Q_MAKERS, UPLIFT or this file: run node .scripts/year-classics/shipped.js "<quote>" "<author>" before proposing, and again before ruling.
Keep the material publishable: no graphic description of wounds, dying or atrocity. A quotation that would need a content warning is the wrong quotation, however powerful.
A confident false citation is worse than an honest "attributed to". Never mint wording. Where the trail runs out, HEDGE with a note that says so plainly.
The editor is forbidden to pad the month to reach the day count.

WHERE TO LOOK WHEN DIARY AND CORRESPONDENCE RUN THIN (the owner's suggestion, 20 September 2026, written in after September left one Diary line in the whole held pool). Three groups the lanes have barely touched, all of whom wrote in exactly the forms that are short. EXPLORERS AND TRAVELLERS, who keep journals: Scott, Shackleton, Nansen, Darwin aboard the Beagle, Ibn Battuta, Mary Kingsley, Isabella Bird, Xuanzang. MUSICIANS, who write letters and memoirs about the work: Mozart, Berlioz, Clara Schumann, Tchaikovsky, Ethel Smyth, Stravinsky on his own art. HEADS OF STATE AND FOUNDERS, in their written books and letters, not on a platform: Nehru to his daughter, Elizabeth the First, Lincoln in a letter, Havel to Olga, Gandhi and Mandela on their own lives. The scope does not move for them: a NAMED WORK published before 2000, the same locatable citation, and no speech and no song, because oratory belongs to the Makers and lyrics are out of scope for everyone. A musician is quoted from prose and a leader from the page, never from the podium.

LANE FLOORS. The fiction-essay lane covers four forms and in February proposed sixteen with one diary line and one letter among them, so the month landed full with Diary and Correspondence at one each: the Makers' dead-lane symptom, from a live lane. From March the fiction-essay lane proposes at least three Diary and at least three Correspondence candidates in its sixteen; the poetry-drama lane at least four Drama; the philosophy lane at least two Essay. A lane that cannot meet its floor says so rather than padding.
outOfScope: scripture and liturgy (the Library owns them)
film and television lines (the lift bank owns them)
proverbs and anonymous traditions (the Philosophers' Wisdom tag owns them)

speeches and oratory (the Makers' ground; re-examined 20 September 2026 when the pool widened to explorers, musicians and heads of state, and kept out: a speech has no stable text, what was delivered and what was printed differ, and its famous lines are the most corrupted in the trade, which is how Kennedy's rewording of Shaw came to be the version everyone carries. A leader is quoted from the page, never from the podium)
anything that would need a content warning

carryIns.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
carryIns.source: Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem) (trans. Alan R. Clarke, 1993)
carryIns.note: Verified in Clarke’s translation with the leading And; Melchizedek speaks it. Hope rather than beginning.

carryIns.quote: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light!
carryIns.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 57, first line (trans. the author, 1912)
carryIns.note: Verified in Tagore’s own English of 1912. A light line for the dark month.

carryIns.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
carryIns.source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave One (Jacob Marley’s Ghost)
carryIns.note: Verified in Stave One with the first-edition commas. A December line by its book.

carryIns.quote: But I maintain that she would come if we worked for her, and that so to work, even in poverty and obscurity, is worth while.
carryIns.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter 6, the closing sentence (1929)
carryIns.note: CORRECTED: a note names her. She is Shakespeare’s sister, the gifted poet Woolf imagines, who died young and never wrote a word. The closing sentence of the book, so December’s by right.

carryIns.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
carryIns.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium, the closing sentence (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
carryIns.note: Verified closing line of the Ethics in Elwes. Carried to March as a discipline line and not used: it merely fits there, and as a closing sentence it belongs to December.

carryIns.quote: All the same I’m not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate. The reason is that my pink cactus is probably going to flower. It’s a very rare plant I’ve been given, and I’m told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.
carryIns.source: Colette, Break of Day, the letter that opens the book, pp. 5 to 6 (Sido, the narrator’s mother) (trans. Enid McLeod, 1961)
carryIns.note: CORRECTED and re-verified: a comma after All the same restored. The printed page is lending restricted, so the punctuation is medium confidence. A flowering that is worth waiting for, which is hope more than renewal.

carryIns.quote: To awaken quite alone in a strange town is one of the pleasantest sensations in the world. You are surrounded by adventure. You have no idea of what is in store for you, but you will, if you are wise and know the art of travel, let yourself go on the stream of the unknown and accept whatever comes in the spirit in which the gods may offer it.
carryIns.source: Freya Stark, Baghdad Sketches, In the Moslem Quarter, opening sentences, p. 17 (John Murray, 1937)
carryIns.note: Verified, and a waking line, which April already had four of. Held for the month of hope.

carryIns.quote: May lily-dotted lakes delight your eye; / May shade-trees bid the heat of noonday cease; / May soft winds blow the lotus-pollen nigh; / May all your path be pleasantness and peace.
carryIns.source: Kālidāsa, Shakuntala, Act IV (Invisible beings) (trans. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
carryIns.note: Verified to the letter, and dropped on rule 2 alone: the refuter could find no standard reference entry for the stanza, and Shakuntala is not known by it. A blessing on someone setting out, so it is offered again in December.

carryIns.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
carryIns.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, Renascence, lines 203 to 206, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917)
carryIns.note: Verified. A poem of being born again, kept whole for the month that is named for it.

carryIns.quote: And the miraculous comes so close / to the ruined, dirty houses— / something not known to anyone at all, / but wild in our breast for centuries.
carryIns.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘Everything is plundered’, lines 9 to 12, Anno Domini MCMXXI (trans. Stanley Kunitz with Max Hayward, 1973)
carryIns.note: Verified at medium confidence. Another Akhmatova is already held for October, so this one goes to December.

carryIns.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
carryIns.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, lines 1 to 5, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
carryIns.note: Verified against reprints crediting Dream Work, no comma before repenting. April landed eight poems and this one is about permission rather than the road.

carryIns.quote: And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
carryIns.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Third Part, On Old and New Tablets, 23 (Zarathustra) (trans. Walter Kaufmann, 1954)
carryIns.note: Verified in Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche, p. 322. Nietzsche stands at two of three and his child at play is also held, so only one of the two can ever land; this is the better of them.

carryIns.quote: You do not have to be good.
carryIns.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, the opening line, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986)
carryIns.note: Verified opening line. Held: you do not have to be good is a door opening, which is December’s promise.

carryIns.quote: Now I become myself.
carryIns.source: May Sarton, Now I Become Myself, line 1, first sentence only, Collected Poems 1930 to 1993 (W. W. Norton, 1993)
carryIns.note: Corrected the locator and the edition, both at medium confidence. Held: now I become myself is a beginning, so December.

carryIns.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
carryIns.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held again: a book that has never finished saying what it has to say is the promise December keeps.

carryIns.quote: The maturity of man—that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
carryIns.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, chapter IV, Apophthegms and Interludes, section 94 (trans. Helen Zimmern, 1907)
carryIns.note: Corrected: Zimmern’s translation is 1907. Held: the seriousness of a child at play is a renewal, and Nietzsche stands at two of three.

carryIns.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
carryIns.source: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, First Act (Lord Darlington)
carryIns.note: Verified, First Act. Held: the inversion is wit about self-knowledge and the play rebukes it in the next line.

carryIns.quote: In every town and every village and every mud hut in the world there is always a man who loves children and who will fight to make a good world for them.
carryIns.source: Lillian Hellman, Watch on the Rhine, Act Three, his farewell to his children (Kurt Müller) (Random House, 1941)
carryIns.note: Corrected wording: the printed play carries the longer form with the three and joined clauses, not the 1943 film version. Held: the Drama lane took three.

carryIns.quote: The fairest action of our human life, / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
carryIns.source: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, the close of Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Chorus) (1613 quarto)
carryIns.note: Corrected: the spelling is modernised from the 1613 quarto but the pointing is the quarto pointing, comma in line 1 and colon in line 2. Held: forbearance rather than endurance.

carryIns.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
carryIns.source: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market, lines 562 to 567, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862) (Laura)
carryIns.note: Verified, the closing lines of the poem. Lifting one who totters is a trial line.

carryIns.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
carryIns.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
carryIns.note: Verified opening line. Held: Mrs Dalloway buying the flowers herself is plain speech about a whole life, and it offers no counsel.

carryIns.quote: In spite of illness, in spite even of the arch-enemy sorrow, one can remain alive long past the usual date of disintegration if one is unafraid of change, insatiable in intellectual curiosity, interested in big things, and happy in small ways.
carryIns.source: Edith Wharton, A Backward Glance, A First Word, third paragraph (D. Appleton-Century, 1934)

carryIns.quote: If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present.
carryIns.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 6.4311 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)

carryIns.quote: We look at the world once, in childhood. / The rest is memory.
carryIns.source: Louise Glück, Nostos, the closing lines, Meadowlands (Ecco Press, 1996)

carryIns.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
carryIns.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 7 (c. 1790 to 1793)
carryIns.note: Verified, the tenth Proverb of Hell, plate 7. Time and what is made in it: an impermanence line more than a discipline line.

carryIns.quote: My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends— / It gives a lovely light!
carryIns.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, First Fig, the whole poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Harper and Brothers, 1922)
carryIns.note: Corrected the edition to the Harper text of 1922. Held: a candle that will not last the night is impermanence.

carryIns.quote: Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.
carryIns.source: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Harper and Brothers, 1916)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: laughter is the weapon here, not endurance, so it wants the lighter month.

carryIns.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
carryIns.source: Bernard Shaw, John Bull’s Other Island, Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly (Peter Keegan)
carryIns.note: Verified as Peter Keegan’s reply to Nora Reilly. Held because the drama lane was already full.

carryIns.quote: Human beings have rights, because they are moral beings: the rights of all men grow out of their moral nature; and as all men have the same moral nature, they have essentially the same rights.
carryIns.source: Angelina Grimké, Letters to Catherine E. Beecher, Letter XII, Human Rights Not Founded on Sex, 2 October 1837 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)

carryIns.quote: As a woman, I have no country. As a woman I want no country. As a woman my country is the whole world.
carryIns.source: Virginia Woolf, Three Guineas, section Three, on ‘our’ country (Hogarth Press, 1938) (the outsider)
carryIns.note: Corrected the locator. The sentences stand in section Three, a page before the Society of Outsiders is named, so that heading was too far on. Woolf puts the words inside quotation marks in the mouth of the outsider, answering a demand that she fight for her country, and the cut raises her lower case as to a capital.

carryIns.quote: Justice is a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will.
carryIns.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, II-II, q. 58, a. 1, I answer that (trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 1920)
carryIns.note: The line stands in the body of article 1, not in a reply to an objection. Aquinas offers it as a reformulation of the Roman jurists’ definition, introduced by if anyone would reduce it to the proper form of a definition, and he endorses it. The lifted clause takes a capital and a full stop.

carryIns.quote: My final prayer: O my body, make of me always a man who questions!
carryIns.source: Frantz Fanon, Black Skin, White Masks, Conclusion, the final sentence (trans. Charles Lam Markmann, 1967)

carryIns.quote: What is wanted for women is equal rights, equal admission to all social privileges; not a position apart, a sort of sentimental priesthood.
carryIns.source: Harriet Taylor Mill, Enfranchisement of Women, Westminster and Foreign Quarterly Review, July 1851, on the Worcester resolutions

carryIns.quote: Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights.
carryIns.source: Olympe de Gouges, Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, Article I (trans. Lynn Hunt, 1996)

carryIns.quote: I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken.
carryIns.source: Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, answering why appeal to women, p. 16 (American Anti-Slavery Society, 1836)
carryIns.note: Corrected: in the 1836 pamphlet the sentence begins To this I reply, and the quotation starts at the clause that follows, every word in order. The page is added: the passage stands on page 16, answering the objection that women make no laws and have no legislative power.

carryIns.quote: Yes, I’d give the Devil benefit of law, for my own safety’s sake.
carryIns.source: Robert Bolt, A Man for All Seasons, Act One, the exchange with Roper (Heinemann, 1960) (Sir Thomas More)

carryIns.quote: Let a new earth rise. Let another world be born.
carryIns.source: Margaret Walker, For My People, the opening of the final stanza, Poetry, November 1937, and For My People (Yale, 1942)

carryIns.quote: Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!
carryIns.source: Anna Laetitia Barbauld, The Rights of Woman, line 1, Works, ed. Lucy Aikin, vol. I, p. 185 (Longman, 1825)
carryIns.note: Corrected the locator to page 185 of the 1825 Works, line 1. The poem was printed after Barbauld died and it turns against its own opening: the last stanza tells woman to abandon each ambitious thought and closes that separate rights are lost in mutual love.

carryIns.quote: Music to soothe all its sorrow, / Till war and crime shall cease; / And the hearts of men grown tender / Girdle the world with peace.
carryIns.source: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, Songs for the People, the closing stanza, Poems (George S. Ferguson, 1896); first in Atlanta Offering, 1895

carryIns.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
carryIns.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, Part One, The Rebel (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
carryIns.note: Verified in Bower with his em dash, the last sentence of Part One; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 3. Camus stands at one for the year.

carryIns.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
carryIns.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
carryIns.note: Verified in Frechtman. Beauvoir stands at one for the year.

carryIns.quote: Yet minds are not conquered by force, but by love and high-mindedness.
carryIns.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Appendix, XI (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
carryIns.note: Verified in Elwes. January routed Spinoza’s closing sentence to March; one Spinoza per month.

carryIns.quote: Here is thy footstool and there rest thy feet where live the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
carryIns.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 10, opening sentence (the author’s own English, 1912)
carryIns.note: Verified in the Macmillan text; a prose poem, so no line breaks. January routed Light, my light to December; one Tagore per month.

carryIns.quote: Yet such is oft the course of deeds that move the wheels of the world: small hands do them because they must, while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.
carryIns.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 2, The Council of Elrond (Elrond) (George Allen and Unwin, 1954), p. 283
carryIns.note: Verified on p. 283 of the 1954 Allen and Unwin text by search-inside; the opening word Yet was outside the snippet and rests on secondary witnesses. Add p. 283 to the source. A service line. Mind the Tolkien count: the carry holds several.

carryIns.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
carryIns.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, the Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
carryIns.note: Verified travel line held: it widens the circle rather than counselling, and Twain is unused in the year.

carryIns.quote: I do not care what case you put; let them be sea-captains, if you will.
carryIns.source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, on the offices women may fill (ed. Arthur B. Fuller, 1855)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: let them be sea-captains is an argument about what is owed to women.

carryIns.quote: If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
carryIns.source: Mary Astell, Some Reflections upon Marriage, the 1706 Preface, printed as the Appendix in the fourth edition, 1730, p. 150
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: Astell’s question is a demand for justice, not counsel.

carryIns.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
carryIns.source: Bertrand Russell, What I Believe, chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), p. 20
carryIns.note: Verified in the Dutton text of 1925. Held: the good life inspired by love and guided by knowledge is a public creed.

carryIns.quote: The door itself / makes no promises. / It is only a door.
carryIns.source: Adrienne Rich, Prospective Immigrants Please Note, closing lines, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (Harper and Row, 1963)
carryIns.note: Corrected publisher: Harper and Row published the book in 1963 and Norton reissued it in 1967.

carryIns.quote: I can’t do much with my hands; so I will make a battering-ram of my head and make a way through this rough-and-tumble world.
carryIns.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, letter to her father of 29 November 1856, p. 89 (ed. Ednah D. Cheney, 1889)
carryIns.note: Corrected: this is not a journal entry of 1850. Cheney prints it in chapter five, Authorship, inside a letter written from Boston to her father on 29 November 1856, her twenty-fourth birthday, on page 89 of the Roberts Brothers edition. The tag becomes Correspondence. The wording is exact.

carryIns.quote: I will not be ‘famous’, ‘great’. I will go on adventuring, changing, opening my mind and my eyes, refusing to be stamped and stereotyped.
carryIns.source: Virginia Woolf, A Writer’s Diary, the entry of 29 October 1933 (ed. Leonard Woolf, Hogarth Press, 1953)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held for a later month.

carryIns.quote: But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
carryIns.source: Sarah Moore Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, Letter II, Woman Subject Only to God, p. 10 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: the Correspondence lane took three and this one belongs with Fuller and Cooper.

carryIns.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
carryIns.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series, Self-Reliance (James Munroe, 1841)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: Trust thyself is self-reliance under pressure more than counsel from an elder.

carryIns.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
carryIns.source: James Baldwin, Nothing Personal, the closing passage (Atheneum, 1964)

carryIns.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
carryIns.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
carryIns.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

carryIns.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
carryIns.source: Kate Chopin, The Awakening, chapter XIX (1899)
carryIns.note: Verified in chapter XIX of 1899. Casting aside the fictitious self, which is a truth line held for want of a day.

carryIns.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
carryIns.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
carryIns.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

carryIns.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
carryIns.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
carryIns.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien’s small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

carryIns.quote: In the highlands you woke up in the morning and thought: Here I am, where I ought to be.
carryIns.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, Kamante and Lulu, ch. 1, The Ngong Farm (Putnam, 1937)
carryIns.note: Corrected the locator. Book One is titled Kamante and Lulu and The Ngong Farm is its first chapter, so the proposal gave the chapter title in the place of the book title. The wording is exact. Blixen wrote the book in English, so no translator is named.

carryIns.quote: This being the case, if I were asked to name the chief benefit of the house, I should say: the house shelters daydreaming, the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace.
carryIns.source: Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space, ch. 1, ‘The House. From Cellar to Garret’, p. 6 (trans. Maria Jolas, 1964)
carryIns.note: Corrected the wording against the Jolas scan at the Internet Archive. The sentence begins This being the case, and the edition spells daydreaming as one word: the hyphen that circulates online is an end of line break in the scan. The page, 6, is added.

carryIns.quote: Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening soil.
carryIns.source: Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus, the Colonus ode, first strophe, from line 668 (the Chorus) (trans. F. Storr, 1912)

carryIns.quote: Thousands at his bidding speed / And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest: / They also serve who only stand and waite.
carryIns.source: John Milton, When I consider how my light is spent, lines 12 to 14, Poems (1673)
carryIns.note: Corrected the edition. The old spellings o’re and waite belong to the Poems of 1673, verified in the Milton Reading Room text of that edition. Beeching’s Oxford text of 1900 was not opened and is not claimed. The quotation begins inside line 12, which opens Is Kingly.

carryIns.quote: Up the dome of heaven / Like a great hill, / I watch them marching / Stately and still, / And I know that I / Am honored to be / Witness / Of so much majesty.
carryIns.source: Sara Teasdale, Stars, the last two stanzas, lines 13 to 20, Flame and Shadow, Part I (Macmillan, 1920)
carryIns.note: Corrected: the poem runs to twenty lines in five stanzas, so its closing two stanzas are lines 13 to 20 and not lines 17 to 24. The wording, capitals and punctuation are those of the 1920 text. The alternating indents of the printed page cannot be shown in a single line.

carryIns.quote: Let it come, as it will, and don’t / be afraid. God does not leave us / comfortless, so let evening come.
carryIns.source: Jane Kenyon, Let Evening Come, the final stanza, lines 16 to 18 (Graywolf Press, 1990)

carryIns.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
carryIns.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, ch. 1, ‘An Unexpected Party’, first sentence
carryIns.note: Verified opening line, pure delight; January had more openings than days. Mind the cap: the Calendar For Life bank carries many Tolkien lines.

carryIns.quote: The time that my journey takes is long and the way of it long. I came out on the chariot of the first gleam of light, and pursued my voyage through the wildernesses of worlds leaving my track on many a star and planet.
carryIns.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 12, opening two paragraphs (trans. the author, 1912)
carryIns.note: Verified. The long journey inward, which suits the month of stillness better than the month of setting out.

carryIns.quote: Men may dyen of ymaginacioun, / So depe may impressioun be take.
carryIns.source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Miller’s Tale, lines 3612 to 3613, The Riverside Chaucer (the Miller)
carryIns.note: Verified in the Riverside lineation. Middle English on the page, which suits a month with room for older spelling.

carryIns.quote: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Publick should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.
carryIns.source: Samuel Johnson, letter to Lord Chesterfield, 7 February 1755, in Boswell, Life of Johnson, under 1755
carryIns.note: Corrected to the wording Boswell prints, with obligations in the plural and Publick in the old spelling. The manuscript behind the Hyde edition differs again.

carryIns.quote: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
carryIns.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, chapter 1, opening sentence (Genly Ai)
carryIns.note: Verified as the first sentence of Genly Ai’s report. Truth as a matter of the imagination, which is a strong line for any month about story.

carryIns.quote: The universe is made of stories, / not of atoms.
carryIns.source: Muriel Rukeyser, The Speed of Darkness, section IX (Random House, 1968)
carryIns.note: Verified in section IX of The Speed of Darkness. Stories rather than atoms, a line about what the world is made of.

carryIns.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
carryIns.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
carryIns.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

carryIns.quote: What is there / like fortitude! What sap / went through that little thread / to make the cherry red!
carryIns.source: Marianne Moore, Nevertheless, the last four lines, in the collection Nevertheless (Macmillan, 1944)
carryIns.note: Corrected: the quotation now starts at What is there, so the verse keeps Moore own line breaks. Held: the Poetry lane was the fattest in the month.

carryIns.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
carryIns.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
carryIns.note: Verified in McDuff. Held because April landed the other Boye, and one person may stand once a month; the pain of growth suits the month of courage.

carryIns.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
carryIns.source: Anne Brontë, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
carryIns.note: Verified in the Preface to the second edition of 1848. A plain statement of purpose.

carryIns.quote: Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.
carryIns.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)

carryIns.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
carryIns.source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, chapter I (trans. Arthur Mitchell, 1911)

carryIns.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
carryIns.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
carryIns.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

carryIns.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
carryIns.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

carryIns.quote: Good prose is like a window pane.
carryIns.source: George Orwell, Why I Write, the final paragraph (Gangrel, No. 4, Summer 1946)
carryIns.note: Verified in the final paragraph of Gangrel, Summer 1946. Held because Orwell can stand once in a month.

carryIns.quote: He that would seriously set upon the search of truth, ought in the first place to prepare his mind with a love of it.
carryIns.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book IV, ch. XIX, Of Enthusiasm, section 1 (ed. Fraser, 1894, vol. II, p. 428)
carryIns.note: Corrected against Fraser’s Clarendon edition of 1894, which keeps the comma after truth. Of Enthusiasm was added in the fourth edition of 1700.

carryIns.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
carryIns.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
carryIns.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

carryIns.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
carryIns.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
carryIns.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

carryIns.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
carryIns.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
carryIns.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

carryIns.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
carryIns.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
carryIns.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

carryIns.quote: Let them a journey new begin, / But I at last with weary feet / Will turn towards the lighted inn, / My evening-rest and sleep to meet.
carryIns.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Return of the King, Book VI, chapter 6, Many Partings (George Allen and Unwin, 1955) (Bilbo Baggins)
carryIns.note: Corrected the tag from Poetry to Fiction. These are the last four lines of the walking song Bilbo murmurs in Rivendell, verse set inside a novel, and The Classics tags such verse by the form of the work. The wording matches every transcription consulted; the 1955 printed page itself was not opened.

carryIns.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
carryIns.source: Horace, Odes, Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5, p. 279 (trans. C. E. Bennett, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
carryIns.note: Verified in Bennett, p. 279. The closing ode of Book III, so it is a closing line: the work that outlasts its maker belongs with the promise the books keep. The same text was carried as 03-cfl-08, which is dropped in favour of this record.

carryIns.quote: Yes, she thought, laying down her brush in extreme fatigue, I have had my vision.
carryIns.source: Virginia Woolf, To the Lighthouse, Part III, section 14, the closing sentence (Lily Briscoe) (Hogarth Press, 1927)
carryIns.note: Corrected the locator. The Hogarth first edition of 1927 misnumbers the sections of The Lighthouse and prints the last one as 14; section XIII is the American numbering. The wording was checked against a scan of the Hogarth text and is unchanged.

carryIns.quote: For now he knew what Shalimar knew: If you surrendered to the air, you could ride it.
carryIns.source: Toni Morrison, Song of Solomon, chapter 15, the closing sentence (Alfred A. Knopf, 1977)
carryIns.note: Verified closing sentence. Held for the month of closing lines: surrender that turns into flight.

carryIns.quote: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
carryIns.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, ch. XIV, the closing sentence, p. 490 (John Murray, 1859)
carryIns.note: Verified closing sentence of the first edition, p. 490, without by the Creator. Held for the month of closing lines: endless forms still being evolved is a beginning.

carryIns.quote: That living word awakened my soul, gave it light, hope, joy, set it free!
carryIns.source: Helen Keller, The Story of My Life, chapter IV, the well-house (Doubleday, Page and Company, 1903)
carryIns.note: Verified. Held: the word that awakened her soul gave it light, hope and joy, which is December’s promise.

carryIns.quote: A sheltered life can be a daring life as well. For all serious daring starts from within.
carryIns.source: Eudora Welty, One Writer’s Beginnings, III, Finding a Voice, the closing lines (Harvard University Press, 1984), p. 104
carryIns.note: Verified in the Harvard text: the last two sentences of the book, p. 104. Held for the month of closing lines.

carryIns.quote: If we had no winter the spring would not be so pleasant: if we did not sometimes tast of adversity, prosperity would not be so welcome.
carryIns.source: Anne Bradstreet, Meditations Divine and Moral, meditation XIV (ed. J. H. Ellis, 1867), p. 51
carryIns.note: Verified on the Ellis page image, p. 51. Held: winter makes the spring pleasant, a renewal line for the winter month.

carryIns.quote: You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat.
carryIns.source: George Herbert, Love (III), lines 17 to 18, The Temple (Cambridge, 1633)
carryIns.note: Verified in two copies of the 1633 printing, closing couplet of the last poem of The Church. A gratitude line.

carryIns.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
carryIns.source: Adrienne Rich, Natural Resources, closing six lines, The Dream of a Common Language (W. W. Norton, 1978)
carryIns.note: Verified against three postings crediting the 1978 edition; the Norton page itself was not opened. A trial line.

carryIns.quote: As firmly cemented clam shells / Fall apart in autumn, / So I must take to the road again, / Farewell, my friends.
carryIns.source: Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, the closing verse at Ogaki (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1966)

# Famous, and not theirs

Pasted into every curator and verifier brief for The Classics. Each line below
travels under a name that did not write it. Propose the real author with the
real source, or leave it out; never the famous name.

| The line | Travels as | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Be the change you wish to see in the world | Gandhi | Not in Gandhi's works in that form. The nearest is a 1913 Indian Opinion passage on personal change reflecting in the world; the slogan is later. |
| Well-behaved women seldom (rarely) make history | Marilyn Monroe, Eleanor Roosevelt | Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, "Vertuous Women Found", American Quarterly 28 (1976). |
| Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results | Einstein | Not Einstein. Earliest in print: a Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet (1981); also in Rita Mae Brown's Sudden Death (1983). |
| What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us | Emerson, Thoreau | Henry Stanley Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940). |
| This too shall pass | Lincoln, Solomon, the Sufis | A Persian adage. Lincoln tells it as an Eastern monarch's story in the Wisconsin State Fair address (1859); it is not his line. |
| Be yourself; everyone else is already taken | Oscar Wilde | Not in Wilde. Twentieth-century, author unknown. |
| I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it | Voltaire | Evelyn Beatrice Hall, The Friends of Voltaire (1906), summarising his attitude. |
| Whatever you can do, or dream you can, begin it. Boldness has genius, power and magic in it | Goethe | John Anster's very free 1835 rendering of the Prelude to Faust; the German has nothing like it. |
| The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing | Edmund Burke | Not in Burke. The closest is John Stuart Mill's 1867 St Andrews address, and that is not the wording either. |
| There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed | Hemingway | Not Hemingway. Traced to sportswriter Red Smith, and not verbatim there. |
| Write drunk, edit sober | Hemingway | Not Hemingway; nearest is Peter De Vries, Reuben, Reuben (1964), about a character. |
| If you want to build a ship, don't drum up the men to gather wood | Saint-Exupéry | A paraphrase; the Citadelle passage says something adjacent and longer. Quote the real passage, in a named translation, or leave it. |
| Dance like nobody's watching | Mark Twain | A 1987 country lyric (Susanna Clark and Richard Leigh, "Come from the Heart"). |
| Not all who wander are lost | Tolkien | Tolkien wrote "Not all those who wander are lost." Already shipped in the lift bank; excluded anyway. |
| The definition of a friend is one soul in two bodies | Aristotle | Diogenes Laërtius reports it of Aristotle, Lives 5.20; cite Diogenes, not Aristotle's works. |
| A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step | Laozi | Real (Tao Te Ching 64) and shipped on the Philosophers; Laozi is banned here anyway. |
| Hell is other people | Sartre | Real (Huis Clos, 1944) but nearly always misread; if proposed, the note must carry Sartre's own gloss. |
| God is dead | Nietzsche | Real (The Gay Science 108, 125) but it is the madman's line and needs the context; not a morning line in any case. |
| The unexamined life is not worth living | Socrates | Real: Plato, Apology 38a, and it is Plato's Socrates. Cite Plato, name the translator. |
| Beauty will save the world | Dostoevsky | Real, but it is Ippolit REPORTING Myshkin in The Idiot, part 3, ch. 5. The speaker goes in the source. |
| To thine own self be true | Shakespeare | Real, but the speaker is Polonius, Hamlet 1.3, and he is not offered as wisdom. Name him. |
| Two roads diverged... I took the one less traveled by | Frost | Real, and shipped in the lift bank; excluded. Frost's own reading of the poem is ironic, which a note would have to say. |
| Do not go gentle into that good night | Dylan Thomas | Real (1951), and grief; publishability decides, and the month. |
| Everything happens for a reason | Aristotle, Marcus | No source. Out. |
| Music is the universal language of mankind | Longfellow | Real, Outre-Mer (1835), but it is prose travel writing, and it is trite. |
| Fortune favours the bold | Virgil | Real (Aeneid 10.284, audentes fortuna iuvat), and it is Turnus, speaking before he dies. Name the speaker or leave it. |

Two speaker traps to carry generally: a line spoken by a character is the
character's, and goes in the source in parentheses after the locator; a line
one character REPORTS of another is the reporter's, and the note says so.
